newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle crew retrieves satellite.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle crew retrieves satellite.

text.p: The U.S. space shuttle Columbia used its long robotic arm to pluck a prototype satellite factory from space on Monday after swooping around it as a second satellite orbited nearby.
"Wake Shield is grappled," astronaut Tamara Jernigan said as the grapple on the end of the 50-foot (17-meter) arm reached out and grabbed the satellite at 9:01 p.m. EST (0201 GMT on Tuesday).

The astronauts then turned off systems on Wake Shield before Jernigan lowered the robot arm to move the device into Columbia's cargo bay as the spacecraft floated about 220 miles (350 km) above South America.

Retrieval of the Wake Shield Facility had been moved up by about three hours from the original schedule so the Orfeus-Spas telescope, an orbiting observatory also deployed by Columbia, would not stray too close to it, NASA officials said.

NASA had never before flown the shuttle in formation with two recoverable satellites. Flight director Al Pennington had said before the mission the task would be "tricky." But NASA officials said everything went according to plan during the complicated rendezvous and retrieval Monday night.

Wake Shield was about 16 miles (26 km) from Orfeus-Spas when Columbia swooped between them and retrieved the stainless steel disk 12 feet (4 metres) in diameter. NASA had said the two satellites had to be separated by at least 12.5 miles (20 km) for a safe operation.
"Congratulations on a flawless rendezvous and a great capture of the Wake Shield satellite," spacecraft communicator Marc Garneau told the crew.

When the astronauts woke up on Monday, they were 23 miles (37 km) ahead of Wake Shield, which Columbia had released on Friday night. The crew moved the orbiter closer to the satellite during the day as they circled far from Earth.

Shuttle commander Cockrell fired Columbia's maneuvering jets at 3:45 p.m. EST (2045 GMT). A second firing took place at 6:46 p.m. EST (2345 GMT) directing the spacecraft toward its final rendezvous with Wake Shield.

Blaring the pop song "Let the Good Times Roll" by the Cars, mission control had awakened the five astronauts one hour earlier than scheduled so they could begin steering the spacecraft for the interception.

Flight officials at Johnson Space Center in Houston then congratulated astronaut Story Musgrave, 61, on exceeding 1,000 hours in space. Musgrave, the oldest person to fly in space, was making his sixth and probably last shuttle flight.
"Story is looking marvelous for a 1,001-hour space traveler," Cockrell, 46, said.
"We just made a beautiful pass over Hawaii. The islands are clear today. No matter how many hours you've got up here, these ones are just as good as the first ones," Musgrave said.

NASA believes the two craft drew unexpectedly close when the Orfeus-Spas telescope encountered more drag than expected from the thin atmosphere 220 miles (355 km) up as it was pointed at its celestial targets.
The telescope had ceased observations on Sunday so it could be turned to reduce the atmosphere's braking effect on it. It resumed its activities at about 5 a.m. EST (1000 GMT) Monday.

Wake Shield was designed to manufacture ultra-pure thin film wafers used to make semiconductors for the electronics industry. They could lead to faster computer chips and better, smaller cellular phones.

NASA officials said they were very pleased with the performance of the space factory during the three days it spent orbiting apart from Columbia. Two earlier Wake Shield missions, during shuttle flights in 1994 and 1995, had only mixed success.
About $29 million has been invested in the Wake Shield project, excluding the costs of each launch.
